Flagey Building, Brussels

Joseph Diongre’s broadcasting house for Belgian radio, nicknamed the paquebot for its ship-like silhouette: curved facades of ribbon windows and a round tower.

Source
Wikipedia: Flagey Building
Creator
Joseph Diongre
Made
1933–1938 (competition 1933, completed 1938)
Style
Streamline Moderne (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Streamlined, civic, nautical
Evidence
Downloaded to a scratch folder and inspected Busoni’s 2013 photograph on Wikimedia Commons at 1280 px. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Joseph Diongre won a 1933 competition and the building was completed in 1938 as the headquarters of the National Institute of Radio Broadcasting (INR/NIR). Wikipedia calls it Streamline Moderne and gives the nickname “paquebot” (packet boat). Studio 4 is a noted concert hall. It is now the Flagey cultural centre. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • A six-storey block with a pale yellow facade curves around the corner of the square in one continuous sweep.
  • Every floor has a continuous ribbon of windows separated by solid horizontal bands of the yellow wall, so the facade reads as stacked horizontal stripes.
  • A round tower rises from the curved corner; each of its floors is a ring of windows under a projecting band, and a lantern and mast sit on top.
  • Small round clocks sit on the facade near the top of the curve. The walls carry no applied ornament.

Why it belongs

Flagey shows a European version of the style: no chrome and no portholes, but curved corners, continuous horizontal bands, and a funnel-like tower make the ship reading.

Borrow

Wrap a corner with one continuous curve and let horizontal bands run unbroken around it.

A stack of rings with projecting edges reads as a streamline tower or a progress indicator.
